transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, to be completely honest, I’m... I'm here because I am at my wit's end. I’ve been trying, really trying, for well over a year now to get someone—anyone, HR, the site director, whoever—to actually look at what's going on and take it seriously. I’ve been a computer support specialist for a

Aside from this situation at work, do you generally find yourself distrustful or suspicious of other people's motives in your life outside of work — for example, with friends, family, or in other past situations?

No, no, not at all. That’s the thing, Dr. Smith, I’m actually a very... I'm a very grounded person. I mean, my wife and I have been married for thirty-two years, and I trust her implicitly. My kids, my neighbors, the guys I play poker with on the third Friday of every month—I don't have any issues with them. None whatsoever. I’m not some, you know, paranoid guy who thinks everyone is out to get him or that the mailman is reading my letters. 

I've always been a straight shooter, very logical. You kind of have to be when you've been in IT as long as I have. I got my bachelor's back in the eighties, right when things were really taking off, and my whole career has been built on looking at the facts, finding the root cause of a system error, and fixing it. I troubleshoot. So I know how to evaluate a situation objectively, and I take people at face value until the data tells me otherwise. 

And I think that’s exactly why this whole thing at the office is driving me so absolutely crazy, because I know the difference between a normal misunderstanding and... well, and this. If this was just me being a generally suspicious person, I wouldn't have lasted three decades in corporate environments, would I? You have to collaborate, you have to trust your team. But when you are looking right at the network logs, and you see the things I'm seeing them do... I mean, I'm just asking for someone to look at the facts of this one specific situation, you know?

When people have offered other explanations for what you've seen in the logs—like a technical glitch or misunderstanding—are you able to seriously consider that they might be right, or do you find you just can't accept any explanation other than that they're deliberately targeting you?

Well, see, that’s exactly the problem, Dr. Smith. I *did* consider those other explanations. I really did. When this all started, I sat down with management, and they pulled up the logs, and they said to me, "Look, it's just the new ticket rotation algorithm, it’s just standard policy." And they brought up the security audits, too, saying, "Oh, it's just a routine sweep, everybody goes through it." And for a minute, I thought, okay, maybe it is a glitch. Maybe the load balancer on the ticketing system is just misconfigured and dumping all the high-priority, unsolvable legacy issues onto my queue by mistake. I mean, I’ve seen systems do weird things. Back in '98, we had a server that would drop packets only when the AC kicked on because of a faulty ground wire. So, I know glitches happen.

But then I started really looking at the data, tracking it day by day, week by week. And you can’t tell me it’s a coincidence that every single time I get assigned a critical failure ticket, there’s a so-called "random" security audit on my workstation within forty-eight hours. It’s not a glitch. They are using the new ticket rotation and those audits to build a paper trail against me. I’ve been trying for over a year to get someone, anyone, to just look at the timeline I put together. I even color-coded the spreadsheets to show the correlation between the impossible deadlines they give me and the disciplinary flags they try to sneak into my file. 

Management just keeps pointing at the same sanitized logs and repeating, "It’s just policy, it’s just policy." But I know how to read raw system data. I know what a targeted query looks like. They are deliberately orchestrating this to make me look incompetent so they have cause to fire me. And no matter how many times I explain the technical impossibility of their "glitch" theory, they just smile that corporate smile and tell me I'm overthinking it. But I'm not. The math doesn't lie, Dr. Smith, even if they do.
Have you ever heard voices or sounds that other people couldn't hear, or seen things that others didn't see, related to this situation or otherwise?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I don't hear voices or see things that aren't there. Like I said, I'm a very grounded, logical person. I deal with tangible things—hardware, software, data packets, server racks. If I hear a sound, it's because a fan bearing is going out on a server in the data center, or maybe a hard drive is clicking because the read/write head is failing. I know what real sounds are, and I know where they come from. I don't have... hallucinations, or whatever you want to call it. 

I don't need to hear voices to know what they're doing to me at work, Dr. Smith. The evidence is right there on the screen in front of me. It's in the timestamps, the IP addresses, the routing tables. I don't have to imagine them plotting against me because they leave a digital footprint every time they do it. They think they're being clever, hiding behind automated systems and policy updates, but they don't realize I can see the underlying architecture of what they're building. 

So, no, my mind isn't playing tricks on me. I'm not sitting alone in my office hearing whispers from the air vents. I'm sitting at my desk, pulling the raw server logs, and watching them manipulate the ticket queues in real-time. It's all right there in black and white—or, well, green and black, depending on which terminal emulator I'm using that day. But the point is, it's real. It's measurable. It's not some... phantom noise in my head. It's just the cold, hard data.

Aside from this situation with your coworkers, has your day-to-day functioning changed at all—are you still able to perform your actual job duties, concentrate on tasks, and keep up with your usual routines at the same level as before?

Well, absolutely. My functioning hasn't slipped one bit, Dr. Smith. I mean, if you were to ask my wife, she'd tell you I'm just as reliable as the day we met. Outside of this whole nightmare with the ticket rotation and those audits, I still keep my house in complete order. Actually, just this past weekend, I spent about four hours out in the garage reorganizing my workbench, sorting all my spare hardware components by generation and bus type, making sure everything is exactly where it needs to be. 

I handle all the bills, too. I have a custom macro set up in my financial spreadsheet that tracks our monthly budget and balances everything down to the penny, and I pay every single bill at least three days before the due date. Never missed one in my life. I help my wife with whatever she needs, running errands, doing the heavy lifting... I just diagnosed and replaced the heating element in our dryer last Tuesday, actually, which saved us a couple hundred bucks on a repair guy. I like keeping things running smoothly. 

And as for the job itself? My ability to actually do the work is as sharp as ever. When I'm actually allowed to just do my job, I handle the technical parts without breaking a sweat. I can sit there and concentrate on debugging a complex network routing issue or writing out a script for six hours straight if I have to. Nobody—not even the management team that's trying to push me out—nobody has ever been able to say my work is sloppy or disorganized. They literally can't. My documentation is flawless. I comment every single line of code I write, I map out every server dependency, I keep my desk completely clear of clutter... I mean, my physical and digital workspaces are pristine. 

So no, my routines haven't changed. I'm operating at exactly the same high level I always have. It's just that now, I have to spend a portion of my perfectly good cognitive bandwidth tracking their administrative games, you know? But my actual day-to-day life? The real work? It's completely solid. Perfectly organized.
